title: QUIC RFC 9000 Path Validation Datagram Floor Runtime Architecture
purpose: Describe the bounded runtime path that keeps RFC 9000 Section 8.2 path-validation datagram construction, retry cadence, PATH_RESPONSE immediacy, same-path response emission, and anti-amplification exceptions owned by one path-local transport seam.
design_summary: PATH_CHALLENGE and PATH_RESPONSE datagrams share a single runtime construction seam. The seam formats the path-validation frame first, computes the RFC 9000 1200-byte padding target, asks the actual path-local anti-amplification state whether the expanded datagram can be sent, and falls back to the unexpanded frame only when the path budget forbids the 1200-byte datagram. Candidate-path PATH_CHALLENGE emission stores exactly one outstanding challenge payload per send, uses the path-validation timer to retry at the existing probe cadence, and does not bundle multiple PATH_CHALLENGE frames into one datagram. PATH_RESPONSE emission remains immediate in the packet-processing transition that received PATH_CHALLENGE, uses the same path identity as the received challenge, and consumes active-path or candidate-path amplification budget according to the path being answered.
data_and_state_considerations: Candidate-path validation state remains the owner of challenge payloads, send counts, and validation deadlines. Datagram padding is derived from frame length and path-local amplification state, not from a separate synthetic budget. The initiator-side PATH_RESPONSE handler validates only responses that arrive on the matching candidate path; responses on other paths are ignored without turning the same-path response rule into an initiator-enforced peer violation.
edge_cases_and_constraints: PATH_CHALLENGE retries can produce multiple challenge frames over time, but each emitted datagram contains exactly one PATH_CHALLENGE frame.
Repeated candidate-path traffic before the validation deadline must not send probes more frequently than the armed path-validation cadence.
Datagrams containing PATH_CHALLENGE or PATH_RESPONSE are not discarded solely because the protected packet is smaller than 1200 bytes.
PATH_RESPONSE emission must be same-transition and same-path unless path-local congestion or anti-amplification state prevents sending.
A PATH_RESPONSE datagram is expanded to 1200 bytes when budget permits and left unexpanded when expansion would exceed the path anti-amplification limit.
The slice does not widen preferred-address migration, multipath scheduling, public migration APIs, or congestion-control pacing policy.
alternatives_considered: Keep PATH_CHALLENGE and PATH_RESPONSE padding in separate branches; rejected because the response branch had already drifted from the challenge branch's 1200-byte floor.

Use QuicAntiAmplificationBudget as a synthetic padding-only budget in the runtime; rejected because the runtime already owns a path-local amplification state and must account for the full datagram it actually sends.
Treat a PATH_RESPONSE arriving on a different path as a protocol violation at the initiator; rejected because RFC 9000 explicitly forbids enforcing that rule at the initiating endpoint.
risks: The current runtime still emits these path-validation effects as internal datagram payloads rather than a full public API migration surface.
The same-path PATH_RESPONSE proof is path-identity based and does not claim multipath path-set validation.
Benchmark coverage for the shared datagram builder remains the existing helper-level path-validation benchmark family rather than a new stable performance baseline.

supplemental_sections.heading: Scope
supplemental_sections.content: This design covers RFC 9000 Section 8.2 path-validation datagram composition and focused runtime behavior for PATH_CHALLENGE/PATH_RESPONSE handling. It deliberately does not claim broader migration policy, endpoint host routing, multipath, public API migration controls, or HTTP/3 behavior.
